title: A telling hole in a Neandertal bone hints at a bitter end

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: Two graduate students discuss a recent archaeology lecture on Neandertal remains and the evidence of injury and care.

script.en: Did you make it to Dr. Harrow's lecture on the Shanidar Neandertal finds yesterday?
I did, but I had to leave early for a lab meeting. I caught the part about the shoulder blade with the puncture wound. She said it was probably made by a wooden spear.
Right. And the wound showed no signs of healing, which suggests the person died around the time of the injury. But what I found more interesting was the broken tooth.
The incisor? I thought that was just damage from the excavation.
No, the tartar buildup showed the tooth had splintered years before death. So the individual lived with a serious facial injury for a long time.
That's remarkable. Surviving that would have required help from others. Dr. Harrow seemed cautious about that conclusion, though.
She was. She said it's speculation, but it's plausible. The person would have had trouble eating and drinking, and would have been in pain at first.
So the same set of remains suggests both violence and care. That's a complex picture of Neandertal behavior.
Exactly. And she pointed out that many ways to die leave no mark on the skeleton at all. So finding evidence of trauma is rare and valuable.
I wonder if the puncture could have been caused by a stone tool instead. Stone-tipped spears usually make a different shape, right?
Yes, a diamond-shaped hole. The round shape points to a wooden spear. The team also compared it with wounds on butchered animal bones and with experiments using re-created Paleolithic weapons.
That's a lot of careful work. I'm sorry I missed the end. Do you have notes I could borrow?
Sure, I'll email them to you tonight.

script.en: Archaeologists studying ancient human remains often face a fundamental challenge: many causes of death leave no trace on the skeleton. This makes any evidence of trauma particularly valuable. A recent analysis of a Neandertal shoulder blade from Shanidar, a famous burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, has provided such evidence. The bone contains a round puncture wound that researchers believe was made by a wooden spear around the time of death. The shape of the hole is important. Stone-tipped spears typically produce diamond-shaped wounds, while wooden spears leave round ones. The team confirmed their hypothesis by comparing the fossil with butchered animal bones and with wounds created experimentally using re-created Paleolithic weapons. But the story does not end with violence. A shattered incisor found with the remains suggests that the individual, named Shanidar A, suffered a serious facial injury years before death. Tartar buildup on the tooth indicates that it had splintered long before the person died, meaning Shanidar A lived with the disability for a considerable period. Given that such an injury would have affected eating and drinking and caused severe initial pain, the researchers speculate that the individual likely needed care from others. This combination of violence and care, they argue, points to complex social behavior among Neandertals. Not everyone is convinced. Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist not involved in the study, calls the remains 'super cool' because they preserve rare evidence of trauma. However, she and others caution that inferring care from skeletal evidence is speculative. The study authors acknowledge this limitation but maintain that the most parsimonious explanation for Shanidar A's survival is that others helped. The debate highlights a broader issue in archaeology: interpreting behavior from incomplete physical evidence is inherently uncertain, yet such finds offer invaluable glimpses into the lives of our extinct relatives.

sections.title: A Telling Hole in a Neandertal Bone Hints at a Bitter End
sections.passage:
The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write in Scientific Reports. But violence is not all this Neandertal may have known. A shattered tooth found with the remains hints that the deceased suffered a facial injury at some point in life. Surviving this injury indicates that Neandertals may have helped each other in times of need, the study authors speculate.

These remains with visible trauma are "super cool," because "there's a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton," says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri who wasn't involved with the study. Neandertals were often injured throughout their lives, probably from hunting. But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids were stabbing and pummeling each other, perhaps intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago.

During an excavation that began in 2019 at Shanidar, the famous Neandertal burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, researchers uncovered remains from at least three previously unknown individuals. The set included ribs, hand bones, teeth and a perforated shoulder bone that probably belonged to a single individual who lived around 75,000 years ago. At first, the team had no idea what caused the hole. "It's so round, it's like, what is it?" recalls Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge.

The team removed the shoulder blade with the surrounding sediment and tested for evidence that roots or insects had damaged the fossil. But that didn't fit the nature of the damage. Instead, they found fragments of bone from the shoulder blade in the dirt that suggested it had been pierced when the individual, named Shanidar A, was alive. The team also didn't see any signs of healing around the puncture wound when they analyzed the bone under the microscope and using X-rays, suggesting that the injury had occurred around the time of death.

The next task was to find out what instrument might have caused the injury. The team compared the puncture with the fossilized remains of butchered animals found alongside human tools, as well as wounds created by archaeologists stabbing animal corpses with re-created Paleolithic weapons. Stone-tipped spears usually create a diamond-shaped hole. Wooden spears, on the other hand, tend to leave round puncture wounds. The team also found a broken incisor alongside the rest of the remains. The tooth was so shattered that Shanidar A probably experienced a serious injury to their face. Tartar buildup suggests that the tooth splintered in half years before Shanidar A died, meaning they lived with their disability for a long time.

"Given it would have affected their ability to eat, to drink — they'd have been in massive amount of pain at first — it's likely [to] have needed some care," Pomeroy says. That one set of remains suggest both violence and care show that Neandertal "behavior is complex," Pomeroy says. "Like us."

long_sentences.en: These remains with visible trauma are “super cool,” because “there’s a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton,” says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri in Columbia who wasn’t involved with the study.

(See our AI policy here .) The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write October 15 in Scientific Reports .

But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids — modern humans and their extinct cousins — were stabbing and pummeling each other, maybe even intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago .
